transcript.author: ted-nordhaus
transcript.about: Conditional support. More room for other species is necessary, but the question is whose land. Habitat loss is driven mostly by excess material and land use in rich countries, much of it drawn from the South. Reasoning by analogy from fair-share arguments: cut Northern throughput first. Fencing off Southern land would only dispossess people who did little to cause the crisis.

interviews.author: edward-o-wilson
interviews.reaction: Habitat loss drives extinction, and only protecting about half of land and sea, in large connected areas that include indigenous lands kept wild, can save most species. Displacement concerns call for securing inhabitants' territories, not for shrinking the target.

interviews.author: ramachandra-guha
interviews.reaction: Half-Earth exports the American wilderness model to the global South, where reserves evict ecosystem people who live with the forest. Protection should begin by curbing the consumption of the omnivores and by securing local forest rights, not by fencing off inhabited land.

interviews.author: ted-nordhaus
interviews.reaction: Leaving much more land to other species is a worthy aim, but it can only come from decoupling: intensive farming, dense cities and land-light energy. A fixed protected half imposed as a limit on development would be unjust and politically doomed.

interviews.author: baptiste-morizot
interviews.reaction: The claim is opposed as a guiding frame. Splitting the Earth into sanctuary and exploited zone keeps the human/nature divide. Living beings like the wolf cross every line, so cohabitation has to be negotiated through diplomacy on shared territory everywhere. Reserves are only one tool.

interviews.author: terry-anderson
interviews.reaction: A fixed political quota of half the Earth is opposed. Land set aside by decree has no owner who bears the cost of neglect. Secure, tradable property rights, private or communal, conserve habitat better, and how much land to protect should follow from those rights.

interviews.author: paul-robbins
interviews.reaction: Opposed as framed. A global set-aside target treats conservation as apolitical. It hides who loses access to enclosed land and who gains, and it leaves the commodity chains that drive habitat loss in place. More protection needs justice and land rights built into it.

interviews.author: joan-martinez-alier
interviews.reaction: Fencing off half the Earth would put the costs on peasants, pastoralists and indigenous peoples in the South, who already defend land in order to live from it. The pressure comes from the North's social metabolism, so cutting that metabolism should come first.

interviews.author: murray-bookchin
interviews.reaction: Fencing off half the Earth treats a social problem as a question of territory. It leaves alone the hierarchy and the grow-or-die market that devour the rest, and it lets states displace people. Protection lasts only under directly democratic communities that rebalance human society with nature.

interviews.author: bruno-latour
interviews.reaction: Setting half the Earth aside repeats the modern split between nature and society. Gaia reacts everywhere and crosses every fence. Other species need spokespersons in a common assembly that decides about all land, not a reserve kept apart from politics.

interviews.author: val-plumwood
interviews.reaction: Splitting the Earth into a protected nature half and a human half repeats the reason/nature dualism. It erases the people who live in so-called wilderness and leaves the other half open to use without limits. The master's denial of dependence must end on all land.

interviews.author: jason-hickel
interviews.reaction: More room for other species is needed, but a global half quota risks fencing off Southern land while Northern overconsumption, the main driver of habitat loss, continues. Reducing rich-country material and land use comes first, as a matter of justice.

interviews.author: john-bellamy-foster
interviews.reaction: Setting aside protected areas cannot repair the metabolic rift. Capitalist agriculture and accumulation keep draining soil and pushing past limits in the half that is left unprotected. The rift has to be closed in the land that people live on and farm.

interviews.author: roger-scruton
interviews.reaction: A planetary quota drawn from above treats places as map units and their people as obstacles. Habitat lasts where those who call the land home protect it through local institutions, property and attachment. Oikophilia does this work, not global targets.

interviews.author: wendell-berry
interviews.reaction: Protecting wild places is good, but fencing off half the Earth leaves the other half to an industrial economy that ruins soil, communities and farming skill. Care has to reach every farm, woodlot and watershed, because how a people farms is how it lives.

interviews.author: timothy-morton
interviews.reaction: The framing is opposed more than habitat protection itself. Splitting Earth into a human half and a Nature half keeps the idea of a pristine elsewhere alive. Hyperobjects like global warming get past every fence, and ecology is a mesh of entangled beings everywhere.

interviews.author: arne-naess
interviews.reaction: Large wild areas where other beings can unfold on their own terms follow from their value apart from human use. A protected half beside an unchanged industrial half is still shallow ecology. Rich societies must cut consumption, and inhabitants must not be evicted.

interviews.author: philippe-descola
interviews.reaction: Setting half the Earth apart for other species assumes naturalism, a nature outside society that can be fenced off. That is only one of four ontologies. Imposing the partition exports the Western divide onto peoples whose forests are societies of persons.

interviews.author: luc-ferry
interviews.reaction: Opposed as framed. Nature has value for humans, not rights against them. Wild areas deserve protection when people decide it democratically, for human and future generations' sake, not as a fixed quota owed to other species that overrides the people living on the land.

interviews.author: johan-rockstrom
interviews.reaction: Biosphere integrity is a planetary boundary already crossed, so much more protection is needed. But the framework fixes no one-half figure. Reserves fail unless climate, nitrogen and land-use boundaries are respected across the whole Earth system.

interviews.author: davi-kopenawa
interviews.reaction: The forest is not empty land to fence off for other species. People, animals and spirits live in it together. The real threat is the hunger for metal and merchandise, so protection means demarcating peoples' territories and stopping the miners, not dividing the Earth.

interviews.author: holmes-rolston
interviews.reaction: Organisms and ecosystems hold value before any human values them, so protecting them is a duty and not a favor. The figure of half is a policy number, but systemic value needs large, connected wild areas. Displacement and consumption elsewhere still need to be dealt with.

interviews.author: vandana-shiva
interviews.reaction: Splitting the Earth into a protected half and a used half repeats the monoculture of the mind. Forests and biodiversity are kept alive by the subsistence work of rural women and local communities. The real threat is maldevelopment, not the people who live with the land.

interviews.author: elinor-ostrom
interviews.reaction: A single global quota imposed from above risks displacing the users who already govern resources well, turning commons into open access. Protection lasts when local users have recognised rights, clear boundaries, and make, monitor and enforce their own rules.

interviews.author: anna-tsing
interviews.reaction: Opposed as framed. Much multispecies life persists in disturbed, inhabited landscapes, and some of it depends on human disturbance. Fencing off half the planet repeats the plantation logic of clearing people out. The task is living together in shared capitalist ruins, not dividing humans from other species.

interviews.author: robin-wall-kimmerer
interviews.reaction: Splitting the Earth into a used half and a fenced-off half repeats the separation of people from land that caused the harm. Care through reciprocity belongs on all land: take only what is given, and give something back.
